Expectation and moments

Notation: new this session

Notation Definition and usage
\(\arg\max\) The value, among all values in a particular set, that maximizes the given expression. For example, \(\operatorname{argmax}_{x \in \mathbb{R}}(-x^2 - 2x + 3) = -1\). Assumes a unique maximum.
\(\arg\min\) The value that minimizes the given expression. For example, \(\operatorname{argmin}_{x \in \mathbb{R}}(x^2 - 4x + 1) = 2\). Assumes a unique minimum.

Three probability density functions

Expected value

Definition 2.1.1 — Expected Value

For a discrete random variable \(X\) with PMF \(f\) the expected value of \(X\) is \[ \mathrm{E}[X] = \sum_x x f(x). \] For a continuous random variable \(X\) with PDF \(f\), the expected value of \(X\) is \[ \mathrm{E}[X] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x f(x)\, dx. \] Regularity conditions in both cases ensure the sums/integrals converge absolutely.

  • An operator: takes a random variable, returns a number
  • The probability-weighted average of the possible values

The regularity condition is absolute integrability: \(\mathrm{E}[|X|] < \infty\). This ensures that the positive and negative parts of the expectation are both finite. Without it, the expression for \(\mathrm{E}[X]\) could require us to subtract infinity from infinity, so the expected value would not be well defined as a finite number.

Distinguish a function of a random variable from an operator on a random variable. A function \(g\) acts on each possible value of \(X\), so \(g(X)\) is another random variable. The expectation operator acts on the random variable and its distribution as a whole, returning a number. Thus, \(\mathrm{E}[g(X)]\) means: first form the random variable \(g(X)\), then apply the expectation operator to summarize its distribution.

Two simple examples

Example 2.1.2 — A Fair Die Roll

\[ \mathrm{E}[X] = \sum_{x=1}^{6} x \cdot \frac{1}{6} = \frac{7}{2}. \]

Note that \(X\) never takes the value \(3.5\). A random variable need not take its expected value with positive probability.

Example 2.1.3 — Bernoulli Distribution

\[ \mathrm{E}[X] = 0 \cdot (1 - p) + 1 \cdot p = p, \] so means of binary variables are probabilities.

Expectations of functions

Theorem 2.1.5 — Expectation of a Function of a Random Variable

If \(X\) is a discrete random variable with PMF \(f\) and \(g\) is a function of \(X\), then \[ \mathrm{E}[g(X)] = \sum_x g(x) f(x). \] If \(X\) is a continuous random variable with PDF \(f\) and \(g\) is a function of \(X\), then \[ \mathrm{E}[g(X)] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} g(x) f(x)\, dx. \]

  • Just weight \(g(x)\) by the original PMF/PDF
  • In general \(\mathrm{E}[g(X)] \neq g(\mathrm{E}[X])\)

This is sometimes called the “law of the unconscious statistician” — people apply it without realizing it’s a theorem. Caution to raise aloud: E[g(X)] ≠ g(E[X]) in general — e.g., E[X²] ≠ (E[X])² unless variance is 0.

Linearity of expectations

Theorem 2.1.9 — Linearity of Expectations

Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be random variables. Then, \(\forall a, b, c \in \mathbb{R}\), \[ \mathrm{E}[aX + bY + c] = a\mathrm{E}[X] + b\mathrm{E}[Y] + c. \]

  • Holds with no assumptions about the relationship between \(X\) and \(Y\) — dependent, independent, \(\ldots\) it doesn’t matter

Linearity, verified

n = 1_000_000
X = rng.integers(1, 7, size=n)          # die roll
Y = X + rng.exponential(size=n)         # strongly dependent on X

print('E[2X + 3Y + 1] ≈', (2 * X + 3 * Y + 1).mean())
print('2E[X]+3E[Y]+1  ≈', 2 * X.mean() + 3 * Y.mean() + 1)
E[2X + 3Y + 1] ≈ 21.505361469279705
2E[X]+3E[Y]+1  ≈ 21.505361469279705
  • Dependence between \(X\) and \(Y\) is irrelevant — linearity doesn’t care

Moments

Definition 2.1.10 — j-th Raw Moment

For a random variable \(X\) and \(j \in \mathbb{N}\), the \(j\)-th raw moment of \(X\) is \(\mu_j' = \mathrm{E}[X^j]\).

Definition 2.1.11 — j-th Central Moment

For a random variable \(X\) and \(j \in \mathbb{N}\), the \(j\)-th central moment of \(X\) is \(\mu_j = \mathrm{E}\left[(X - \mathrm{E}[X])^j\right]\).

  • The first raw moment is the expected value;
    • the first central moment is always zero
  • The second central moment has its own name…

Variance

Definition 2.1.12 — Variance

The variance of a random variable \(X\) is \[ \mathrm{V}[X] = \mathrm{E}\left[(X - \mathrm{E}[X])^2\right]. \]

Since \(\mathrm{E}[X]\) is a constant, expand the square and apply linearity: \[ \begin{aligned} \mathrm{V}[X] &= \mathrm{E}\left[X^2 - 2X\mathrm{E}[X] + \mathrm{E}[X]^2\right] \\ &= \mathrm{E}[X^2] - 2\mathrm{E}[X]^2 + \mathrm{E}[X]^2 \\ &= \mathrm{E}[X^2] - \mathrm{E}[X]^2. \end{aligned} \]

Variance and standard deviation

Theorem 2.1.13 — Alternative Formula for Variance

For a random variable \(X\), \[ \mathrm{V}[X] = \mathrm{E}[X^2] - \mathrm{E}[X]^2. \]

Definition 2.1.15 — Standard Deviation

\[\sigma[X] = \sqrt{\mathrm{V}[X]}\]

Die roll example

For a fair die, \(\mathrm{E}[X] = 3.5\). Therefore, \[ \begin{aligned} \mathrm{V}[X] &= \frac{1}{6}\sum_{x=1}^{6}\left(x - 3.5\right)^2 = \tfrac{1}{6}\left(2\cdot 2.5^2 + 2\cdot 1.5^2 + 2\cdot 0.5^2\right) \\ & = \tfrac{35}{12} \approx 2.92 \end{aligned} \]

Note also that \[\E[X^2] = \tfrac{1}{6}(1 + 2^2 + 3^2 + 4^2 + 5^2 + 6^2) = \tfrac{91}{6},\]

so \(\V[X] = \E[X^2] - \E[X]^2 = \tfrac{91}{6} - \tfrac{49}{4} = \tfrac{35}{12}.\)

Die roll moments in python

X = stats.randint(1, 7)  # fair die: values 1 through 6
mean = X.moment(1)
second_moment = X.moment(2)

print('E[X] =', mean)
print('E[X²] =', second_moment)
print('V[X] from deviations =', X.expect(lambda x: (x - mean) ** 2))
print('V[X] from moments =', second_moment - mean ** 2)
E[X] = 3.5
E[X²] = 15.166666666666666
V[X] from deviations = 2.9166666666666665
V[X] from moments = 2.916666666666666

How variance and SD transform

Theorems 2.1.14 and 2.1.16 — Properties of Variance and Standard Deviation

For a random variable \(X\), and \(a, c \in \mathbb{R}\),

  • \(\mathrm{V}[X + c] = \mathrm{V}[X]\) and \(\mathrm{V}[aX] = a^2 \mathrm{V}[X]\)
  • \(\sigma[X + c] = \sigma[X]\) and \(\sigma[aX] = |a|\, \sigma[X]\)
  • a shift doesn’t change the spread of a random variable
  • but scaling does:
    • scales SD linearly, but variance increases quadratically

Example 2.1.17: die roll has V[X] = 35/12 ≈ 2.92, σ ≈ 1.71. Multiply faces by 100: variance blows up to ≈29,200 but σ ≈ 171 stays interpretable — why practitioners quote SDs, not variances.

Exercise

Let \(X \sim B(p)\). What is the variance of \(X\)?

Because \(X\) is either 0 or 1, \(X^2 = X\). Thus \(\E[X^2] = \E[X] = p\), and \(\V[X] = \E[X^2] - \E[X]^2 = p - p^2 = p(1-p)\).

Chebyshev’s inequality

Theorem 2.1.18 — Chebyshev’s Inequality

Let \(X\) be a random variable with finite \(\sigma[X] > 0\). Then, \(\forall \epsilon > 0\), \[ \Pr\big[|X - \mathrm{E}[X]| \geq \epsilon\, \sigma[X]\big] \leq \frac{1}{\epsilon^2}. \]

  • Knowing only the mean and SD bounds the tails for any distribution
  • At most \(\frac{1}{4}\) of probability lies beyond 2 SDs; at most \(\frac{1}{9}\) beyond 3 SDs

Chebyshev’s inequality gives a direct proof of the weak Law of Large Numbers. Let \(X_1, \ldots, X_n\) be IID with mean \(\mu\) and finite variance \(\sigma^2\). Then the sample mean \(\bar{X}_n\) has mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2/n\). For any fixed tolerance \(a > 0\), Chebyshev’s inequality gives \[ \Pr\left[|\bar{X}_n - \mu| \geq a\right] \leq \frac{\sigma^2}{n a^2} \longrightarrow 0. \] Thus, as the sample grows, the probability that the sample mean differs from \(\mu\) by at least \(a\) goes to zero. This is convergence in probability, which is the conclusion of the weak Law of Large Numbers.

How tight is Chebyshev?

tight = stats.rv_discrete(values=([-2, 0, 2], [1/8, 3/4, 1/8]))
dists = {'normal': stats.norm(), 'uniform': stats.uniform(),
         'exponential': stats.expon(), 'three-point': tight}

print('eps=2: bound = 0.25')
for name, d in dists.items():
    m, s = d.mean(), d.std()
    actual = d.expect(lambda x: np.abs(x - m) >= 2 * s)
    print(f'  {name:12s} actual = {actual:.4f}')
eps=2: bound = 0.25
  normal       actual = 0.0455
  uniform      actual = 0.0000
  exponential  actual = 0.0498
  three-point  actual = 0.2500
  • Familiar distributions fall well below the bound
  • The specially constructed 3-point distribution attains it exactly

The normal distribution

Definition 2.1.19 — Normal Distribution

A continuous random variable \(X\) follows a normal distribution if it has PDF \[ f(x) = \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-\frac{(x - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}}, \; \forall x \in \mathbb{R}, \] for some constants \(\mu, \sigma \in \mathbb{R}\) with \(\sigma > 0\). We write \(X \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)\).

Theorem 2.1.20 — Mean and Standard Deviation of the Normal Distribution

If \(X \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)\), then \(\mathrm{E}[X] = \mu\) and \(\sigma[X] = \sigma\).

  • Two parameters characterize the distribution:
    • \(\mu\) shifts it and \(\sigma\) scales it

Normals stay normal

Theorem 2.1.21 — Properties of the Normal Distribution

Suppose \(X \sim N(\mu_X, \sigma_X^2)\) and \(Y \sim N(\mu_Y, \sigma_Y^2)\). Then

  • \(\forall a, b \in \mathbb{R}\) with \(a \neq 0\), if \(W = aX + b\), then \(W \sim N(a\mu_X + b, a^2\sigma_X^2)\).
  • If \(X \perp\!\!\!\perp Y\) and \(Z = X + Y\), then \(Z \sim N(\mu_X + \mu_Y, \sigma_X^2 + \sigma_Y^2)\).
  • Linear combinations of independent normals are normal
  • Standardizing: \(\frac{X - \mu}{\sigma} \sim N(0, 1)\)

A question

You must guess the value of a random variable \(X\) before it is drawn, and you’ll be penalized by the squared error of your guess.

What single number should you guess?

  • The most likely value? The middle value? Something else?
  • Does your answer depend on the distribution’s shape?

Mean squared error

Definition 2.1.22 — Mean Squared Error (MSE) about c

For a random variable \(X\) and \(c \in \mathbb{R}\), the mean squared error of \(X\) about \(c\) is \(\mathrm{E}\left[(X - c)^2\right]\).

Theorem 2.1.23 — Alternative Formula for MSE

For a random variable \(X\) and \(c \in \mathbb{R}\), \[ \mathrm{E}\left[(X - c)^2\right] = \mathrm{V}[X] + (\mathrm{E}[X] - c)^2. \]

  • MSE = irreducible variance + squared bias of our guess

The answer: the expected value

Theorem 2.1.24 — The Expected Value Minimizes MSE

The value of \(c\) that minimizes the MSE of r.v. \(X\) about \(c\) is \(c = \mathrm{E}[X]\).

X = rng.exponential(size=200_000)       # skewed: E[X]=1, median≈0.69

cs = np.linspace(0.2, 2.0, 100)
mse = [((X - c) ** 2).mean() for c in cs]
print('argmin MSE ≈', cs[np.argmin(mse)], '   E[X] ≈', X.mean())
argmin MSE ≈ 1.0    E[X] ≈ 0.9998875768385554
  • Even for a skewed distribution, the mean—not the median or mode—is best under squared error
  • Exercise: what if we minimize mean absolute deviation instead?

Easy to prove using previous theorem 2.1.23.

Good discussion: under absolute error the median wins instead. The choice of loss function determines the best predictor — squared loss is a convention with consequences, not a law of nature.

Expectation and moments recap

  • Expectation: probability-weighted average; linear regardless of dependence
  • Variance/SD measure spread; SD preserves the scale of the data
  • Chebyshev: mean + SD bound the tails of any distribution
  • The normal is closed under linear combinations; \((\mu, \sigma)\) are all we need to know
  • \(\mathrm{E}[X]\) is the best constant predictor under MSE

Reading: FoAS Ch. 2 (§2.2–2.3)

Covariance

Definition 2.2.1 — Covariance

The covariance of two random variables \(X\) and \(Y\) is \[ \operatorname{Cov}[X, Y] = \mathrm{E}\big[(X - \mathrm{E}[X])(Y - \mathrm{E}[Y])\big]. \]

Theorem 2.2.2 — Alternative Formula for Covariance

For random variables \(X\) and \(Y\), \[ \operatorname{Cov}[X, Y] = \mathrm{E}[XY] - \mathrm{E}[X]\mathrm{E}[Y]. \]

  • Asks whether \(X\) and \(Y\) move together (linearly). Note that \(\operatorname{Cov}[X, X] = \V[X]\).

The variance rule

Theorem 2.2.3 — Variance Rule

Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be random variables. Then \[ \mathrm{V}[X + Y] = \mathrm{V}[X] + 2\operatorname{Cov}[X, Y] + \mathrm{V}[Y]. \] More generally, \(\forall a, b, c \in \mathbb{R}\), \[ \mathrm{V}[aX + bY + c] = a^2\mathrm{V}[X] + 2ab\operatorname{Cov}[X, Y] + b^2\mathrm{V}[Y]. \]

  • Variances are not linear — the cross term drives diversification, clustering, and much else
  • Mnemonic: \((x + y)^2 = x^2 + 2xy + y^2\)

Correlation

Definition 2.2.5 — Correlation

The correlation of two random variables \(X\) and \(Y\) with \(\sigma[X] > 0\) and \(\sigma[Y] > 0\) is \[ \rho[X, Y] = \frac{\operatorname{Cov}[X, Y]}{\sigma[X]\sigma[Y]}. \] Correlation is scale-free.

Correlated data

Correlation and linear dependence

Theorem 2.2.6 — Correlation and Linear Dependence

For random variables \(X\) and \(Y\),

  • \(\rho[X, Y] \in [-1, 1]\).
  • \(\rho[X, Y] = 1 \iff \exists\, a, b \in \mathbb{R}\) with \(b > 0\) such that \(Y = a + bX\).
  • \(\rho[X, Y] = -1 \iff \exists\, a, b \in \mathbb{R}\) with \(b > 0\) such that \(Y = a - bX\).

Independence kills covariance

Theorem 2.2.8 — Implications of Independence (Part II)

If \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent random variables, then

  • \(\mathrm{E}[XY] = \mathrm{E}[X]\mathrm{E}[Y]\).
  • Covariance is zero: \(\operatorname{Cov}[X, Y] = 0\).
  • Correlation is zero: \(\rho[X, Y] = 0\).
  • Variances are additive: \(\mathrm{V}[X + Y] = \mathrm{V}[X] + \mathrm{V}[Y]\).

A question

We just saw: independence \(\Rightarrow\) zero correlation.

Does zero correlation imply independence?

  • If yes: why?
  • If no: construct a counterexample — two variables with \(\rho = 0\) that are clearly related

No: zero correlation ≠ independence

Example 2.2.9 — Zero Correlation Does Not Imply Independence

Let \(X\) take values \(\{-1, 0, 1\}\) with probability \(\frac{1}{3}\) each, and let \(Y = X^2\). Then \(Y\) is a deterministic function of \(X\), yet \(\operatorname{Cov}[X, Y] = \mathrm{E}[XY] - \mathrm{E}[X]\mathrm{E}[Y] = 0 - 0 = 0\).

X = rng.integers(-1, 2, size=1_000_000)
Y = X ** 2

print('corr(X, Y)     ≈', np.corrcoef(X, Y)[0, 1].round(4))
print('E[Y | X = 0]   =', Y[X == 0].mean(), '  E[Y | X = ±1] =', Y[X != 0].mean())
corr(X, Y)     ≈ 0.0001
E[Y | X = 0]   = 0.0   E[Y | X = ±1] = 1.0
  • Correlation sees only linear structure; the dependence here is perfectly symmetric, so it cancels

Zero correlation can hide patterns

But also: causation \(\not\Rightarrow\) correlation

→ More discussion on this blog

Conditional expectation

Definition 2.2.10 — Conditional Expectation

For discrete random variables \(X\) and \(Y\) with joint PMF \(f\), the conditional expectation of \(Y\) given \(X = x\) is \[ \mathrm{E}[Y \mid X = x] = \sum_y y f_{Y \mid X}(y \mid x), \; \forall x \in \operatorname{Supp}[X]. \] For jointly continuous random variables \(X\) and \(Y\) with joint PDF \(f\), \[ \mathrm{E}[Y \mid X = x] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} y f_{Y \mid X}(y \mid x)\, dy, \; \forall x \in \operatorname{Supp}[X]. \]

  • Expected value computed using conditional distribution: the long-run average of \(Y\) among draws where \(X = x\)

The conditional expectation function

Definition 2.2.15 — Conditional Expectation Function (CEF)

For random variables \(X\) and \(Y\) with joint PMF/PDF \(f\), the conditional expectation function of \(Y\) given \(X = x\) is \[ G_Y(x) = \mathrm{E}[Y \mid X = x], \; \forall x \in \operatorname{Supp}[X]. \]

  • One function collecting every conditional expectation
  • \(\mathrm{E}[Y \mid X]\) denotes \(G_Y(X)\): a random variable whose value is determined by \(X\)

Example 2.2.16 (coin & die): E[Y|X=0] = 5/2 (4-sided), E[Y|X=1] = 7/2 (6-sided). So E[Y|X] is a random variable taking value 5/2 or 7/2 with probability ½ each. Also define conditional variance V[Y|X=x] (Def 2.2.12) analogously.

The Law of Iterated Expectations

Theorem 2.2.17 — Law of Iterated Expectations

For random variables \(X\) and \(Y\), \[ \mathrm{E}[Y] = \mathrm{E}\big[\mathrm{E}[Y \mid X]\big]. \]

  • \(\E[Y \mid X]\) answers “what would I expect \(Y\) to be if I knew \(X\)?” Since we don’t yet know \(X\), this answer is itself a random variable.
  • The LIE says that averaging these conditional forecasts over all possible values of \(X\) gives the unconditional forecast: \(\E\big[\E[Y \mid X]\big] = \E[Y]\).
  • Equivalently: my best guess today of what I’ll forecast once I learn \(X\) is just my forecast today.

More precisely, we mean \[ \mathrm{E}_Y[Y] = \mathrm{E}_X\Big[\mathrm{E}_{Y \mid X}[Y \mid X]\Big]. \]

Law of Iterated Expectations example

n = 1_000_000
X = (rng.random(n) < 0.5).astype(int)                    # coin
Y = np.where(X == 0, rng.integers(1, 5, n), rng.integers(1, 7, n))

print('E[Y]              ≈', Y.mean())
print('E[E[Y|X]] = ½·5/2 + ½·7/2 =', 0.5 * 2.5 + 0.5 * 3.5)
E[Y]              ≈ 2.999794
E[E[Y|X]] = ½·5/2 + ½·7/2 = 3.0

The Law of Total Variance

  • The law of total variance (Thm 2.2.18) splits total uncertainty about \(Y\) into two pieces: \[ \text{Var}(Y) = \underbrace{E\big[\text{Var}(Y \mid X)\big]}_{\text{uncertainty left after learning } X} + \underbrace{\text{Var}\big(E[Y \mid X]\big)}_{\text{uncertainty about what my forecast will be}} \]
    • First term: Noise that knowing \(X\) can’t remove, averaged over possible values of \(X\)
    • Second term: How much my forecast of \(Y\) moves around as \(X\) changes. This is the part of the variation in \(Y\) that \(X\) explains.
  • Learning \(X\) can only remove uncertainty: \(E\big[\text{Var}(Y \mid X)\big] \le \text{Var}(Y)\).
  • \(\text{Var}(Y \mid X)\) answers “how uncertain would I still be about \(Y\) if I knew \(X\)?”
    • Like \(E[Y \mid X]\), this is a random variable, because we don’t yet know \(X\).
  • This is the population version of the ANOVA decomposition
  • Total variability of \(Y\) = average variability of \(Y\) within values of \(X\) + variability of the average of \(Y\) across values of \(X\)

Deviations from the CEF

Theorem 2.2.19 — Properties of Deviations from the CEF

Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be random variables and let \(\varepsilon = Y - \mathrm{E}[Y \mid X]\). Then

  • \(\mathrm{E}[\varepsilon \mid X] = 0\).
  • \(\mathrm{E}[\varepsilon] = 0\).
  • If \(g\) is a function of \(X\), then \(\operatorname{Cov}[g(X), \varepsilon] = 0\).
  • \(\mathrm{V}[\varepsilon \mid X] = \mathrm{V}[Y \mid X]\).
  • \(\mathrm{V}[\varepsilon] = \mathrm{E}[\mathrm{V}[Y \mid X]]\).
  • What’s left after subtracting the CEF is pure noise with respect to \(X\) — uncorrelated with any function of it

The CEF is the best predictor

Theorem 2.2.20 — The CEF is the Best Predictor

For random variables \(X\) and \(Y\), the CEF, \(\mathrm{E}[Y \mid X]\), is the best (minimum MSE) predictor of \(Y\) given \(X\).

  • Earlier today: the best constant guess is \(\mathrm{E}[Y]\)
  • Now: best function of \(X\) is \(\mathrm{E}[Y \mid X]\) — no assumptions
  • But: without assumptions, the CEF can be quite complicated
    • Later you’ll see that linear regression imposes a linear structure on the CEF, which is often a good approximation

The best linear predictor

Theorem 2.2.21 — Best Linear Predictor (BLP)

For random variables \(X\) and \(Y\), if \(\mathrm{V}[X] > 0\), then the best (minimum MSE) linear predictor of \(Y\) given \(X\) is \(g(X) = \alpha + \beta X\), where \[ \alpha = \mathrm{E}[Y] - \frac{\operatorname{Cov}[X, Y]}{\mathrm{V}[X]}\mathrm{E}[X], \qquad \beta = \frac{\operatorname{Cov}[X, Y]}{\mathrm{V}[X]}. \]

Theorem 2.2.22 — Properties of Deviations from the BLP

Let \(\varepsilon = Y - g(X)\), where \(g(X)\) is the BLP. Then \(\mathrm{E}[\varepsilon] = 0\), \(\mathrm{E}[X\varepsilon] = 0\), and \(\operatorname{Cov}[X, \varepsilon] = 0\).

Note the asymmetry vs. the CEF: for the BLP we get only E[ε] = 0, not E[ε|X] = 0. These β and α formulas are population objects — no data, no regression yet. This is the inferential target that regression would estimate (the skipped Ch. 4); we use the BLP as a summary, not an estimator.

CEF vs. BLP

n = 2_000
X = rng.random(n)                       # U(0,1)
Y = 10 * X ** 2 + rng.standard_normal(n)

b = np.cov(X, Y)[0, 1] / X.var()        # sample analogs of beta, alpha
a = Y.mean() - b * X.mean()

xs = np.linspace(0, 1, 100)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.4))
ax.plot(X, Y, '.', ms=2, alpha=0.3)
ax.plot(xs, 10 * xs ** 2, 'k', lw=2, label=r'CEF: $10x^2$')
ax.plot(xs, a + b * xs, 'r', lw=2, label=f'BLP: {a:.2f} + {b:.2f}x')
ax.set(xlabel='x', ylabel='y')
ax.legend()
plt.show()
  • Example 2.2.23: true BLP is \(-\frac{5}{3} + 10X\) — the line tracks the curve as well as any line can

The BLP depends on the dist’n of X

  • With a nonlinear CEF, changing the distribution of \(X\) changes the BLP (Example 2.2.24)
  • The BLP is a property of the joint distribution, not of the CEF alone
  • Practical warning: a “slope” estimated where data are dense may extrapolate badly where data are sparse

Independence, again

Theorem 2.2.25 — Implications of Independence (Part III)

If \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent random variables, then

  • \(\mathrm{E}[Y \mid X] = \mathrm{E}[Y]\).
  • \(\mathrm{V}[Y \mid X] = \mathrm{V}[Y]\).
  • The BLP of \(Y\) given \(X\) is \(\mathrm{E}[Y]\).
  • Under independence, conditioning is useless: the best prediction ignores \(X\) entirely

Covariance matrices

Definition 2.3.1 — Covariance Matrix

For a random vector \(\mathbf{X}\) of length \(K\), the covariance matrix \(\mathrm{V}[\mathbf{X}]\) is the matrix whose \((k, k')\)-th entry is \(\operatorname{Cov}[X_{[k]}, X_{[k']}]\).

\[ \mathrm{V}[\mathbf{X}] = \begin{pmatrix} \V[X_1] & \operatorname{Cov}[X_1, X_2] & \cdots & \operatorname{Cov}[X_1, X_K] \\ \operatorname{Cov}[X_2, X_1] & \V[X_2] & \cdots & \operatorname{Cov}[X_2, X_K] \\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ \operatorname{Cov}[X_K, X_1] & \operatorname{Cov}[X_K, X_2] & \cdots & \V[X_k] \end{pmatrix} \]

  • The covariance matrix is symmetric; the diagonal entries are the variances of the individual components.
  • CEF and BLP generalize to many explanatory variables the same way — multivariate statements mirror the bivariate ones
